paras: The Avoyelles Parish night riding of 1920 was a campaign by night riders who drove Black residents away from several communities in Avoyelles Parish, Louisiana, on or before August 15, 1920. No deaths or injuries were reported, and a meeting of more than two hundred men denounced the practice. The only known account appeared in the Dallas Express, a Black weekly.

According to a dispatch dated August 15, night riders engaged in "fright-training and chasing Negroes" in the parish. The text, badly garbled in the surviving copy, names the places affected as "Markville, Mansour and Bord-on-Sea," apparently Marksville, Mansura and Bordelonville. It also refers to "working Negroes" and to "members of the clan," but neither phrase is clear enough to identify the riders or their motive. The dispatch gives no names of those driven out, no count, and no date for the riding itself.

More than two hundred men attended a meeting that described the practice as "cowardly and thoughtless." The meeting referred the matter to its chairman, a man named Coco, and to Senator A. G. Boyer. No report of arrests, an investigation or any further action appears in the coverage.

The Dallas Express printed the item on page 6 of its August 28, 1920, issue under the headline "Night Riders in Avoyelles Drive, Negroes Away." By placing the meeting's condemnation in the same report, the paper presented the riding as an outrage that local men had publicly repudiated. No account of the episode was found in the white press, and no other Black paper is known to have carried it.
